# A Short R Refresher {#sec-94-r-primer}



For readers who have not written R recently. This is not an introduction to
the language — @wickham2023 is — but the base R that the chapters lean on
without comment: vectors and names, matrices, functions, the `apply()` family,
and the one habit the book insists on, indexing by name. Everything
tidyverse-specific is in @sec-01-setting-up-theory; everything about the
time-series matrix the optimizer wants is in @sec-01-setting-up-implementation.

## Vectors, and their names {.unnumbered}

A vector is the basic object, and a named vector is the object the book uses
for weights. Names are what make a weight vector safe to combine with a return
matrix: the pairing is by name, never by position.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
w <- c(US_equity = 0.4, US_government = 0.5, GLOBAL_commodity = 0.1)
w
#>        US_equity    US_government GLOBAL_commodity 
#>              0.4              0.5              0.1
sum(w)
#> [1] 1
w["US_government"]                 # by name
#> US_government 
#>           0.5
w[c("GLOBAL_commodity", "US_equity")]   # in any order, still right
#> GLOBAL_commodity        US_equity 
#>              0.1              0.4
w * 2                              # arithmetic is elementwise
#>        US_equity    US_government GLOBAL_commodity 
#>              0.8              1.0              0.2
```
:::


Reordering a vector by name is the idiom that appears in almost every chapter:
`w <- w[colnames(R)]` puts a weight vector into the column order of a return
matrix, and `stopifnot(identical(names(w), colnames(R)))` fails loudly if a
name is missing rather than silently pairing the wrong two things.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
cols <- c("GLOBAL_commodity", "US_equity", "US_government")
w2 <- w[cols]
stopifnot(identical(names(w2), cols))
w2
#> GLOBAL_commodity        US_equity    US_government 
#>              0.1              0.4              0.5
```
:::


Logical vectors select; `which()` turns them into positions; `%in%` tests
membership.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
w > 0.2
#>        US_equity    US_government GLOBAL_commodity 
#>             TRUE             TRUE            FALSE
w[w > 0.2]
#>     US_equity US_government 
#>           0.4           0.5
names(w)[w > 0.2]
#> [1] "US_equity"     "US_government"
c("US_equity", "JP_equity") %in% names(w)
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE
```
:::


## Matrices {.unnumbered}

A return matrix has one row per date and one column per asset. `%*%` is matrix
multiplication, `t()` the transpose, `solve()` the inverse (or, better, the
solution of a linear system), and `diag()` both extracts and builds a diagonal.
The portfolio variance $\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}$ of
@sec-02-notation-and-data-notation is three characters of R.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1)
R <- matrix(rnorm(12, sd = 0.03), nrow = 4,
            dimnames = list(NULL, c("A", "B", "C")))
R
#>              A         B         C
#> [1,] -0.018794  0.009885  0.017273
#> [2,]  0.005509 -0.024614 -0.009162
#> [3,] -0.025069  0.014623  0.045353
#> [4,]  0.047858  0.022150  0.011695
S <- cov(R)
w <- c(A = 0.5, B = 0.3, C = 0.2)
as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w)        # portfolio variance
#> [1] 0.0003286
solve(S) %*% rep(1, 3)              # Sigma^-1 iota, the numerator of the GMV weights
#>    [,1]
#> A  3787
#> B -4077
#> C  7332
diag(S)                             # the variances
#>         A         B         C 
#> 0.0010933 0.0004288 0.0005048
```
:::


Column and row operations use `colMeans()`, `rowSums()` and `apply()`; the
second argument of `apply()` is 1 for rows and 2 for columns.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
colMeans(R)
#>        A        B        C 
#> 0.002376 0.005511 0.016290
apply(R, 2, sd)
#>       A       B       C 
#> 0.03306 0.02071 0.02247
apply(R, 1, function(r) sum(w * r))   # a portfolio return per period
#> [1] -0.0029765 -0.0064619  0.0009231  0.0329132
```
:::


## Functions {.unnumbered}

A function bundles a calculation so it can be applied to many series. Default
arguments make an assumption visible and changeable rather than buried.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ann_vol <- function(x, periods = 12) stats::sd(x) * sqrt(periods)
ann_vol(R[, "A"])
#> [1] 0.1145
ann_vol(R[, "A"], periods = 52)
#> [1] 0.2384
```
:::


`sapply()` and `vapply()` apply a function over a vector or list; `vapply()`
declares the type of result it expects and is the one to use in code that must
not fail quietly. `lapply()` returns a list; `Map()` walks several arguments in
parallel.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
vapply(colnames(R), function(s) ann_vol(R[, s]), numeric(1))
#>       A       B       C 
#> 0.11454 0.07174 0.07783
Map(function(name, weight) paste(name, weight), names(w), w)
#> $A
#> [1] "A 0.5"
#> 
#> $B
#> [1] "B 0.3"
#> 
#> $C
#> [1] "C 0.2"
```
:::


## Data frames and tibbles {.unnumbered}

A data frame holds columns of different types; a tibble is a data frame with
better printing. The book builds every figure from one of these, with one row
per plotted thing, and filters it by a `kind` column.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
pts <- tibble::tibble(
  label = c("A", "B", "C", "portfolio"),
  vol   = c(apply(R, 2, sd), sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w))),
  ret   = c(colMeans(R), sum(w * colMeans(R))),
  kind  = c("asset", "asset", "asset", "portfolio")
)
pts
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   label        vol     ret kind     
#>   <chr>      <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>    
#> 1 A         0.0331 0.00238 asset    
#> 2 B         0.0207 0.00551 asset    
#> 3 C         0.0225 0.0163  asset    
#> 4 portfolio 0.0181 0.00610 portfolio
pts[pts$kind == "portfolio", ]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   label        vol     ret kind     
#>   <chr>      <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>    
#> 1 portfolio 0.0181 0.00610 portfolio
```
:::


## Control flow, and where it is avoided {.unnumbered}

`for` loops are fine and the rolling windows of the book are written as loops.
The idiom to remember is to preallocate the result and to fill it by index, and
to fail rather than skip when a step goes wrong.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
win <- 2L
out <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(R))
for (t in (win + 1):nrow(R)) {
  est <- R[(t - win):(t - 1), , drop = FALSE]
  out[t] <- sum(w * colMeans(est))
}
out
#> [1]        NA        NA -0.004719 -0.002769
```
:::


`tryCatch()` captures an error so that a loop can record a failure instead of
dying, which is how @sec-25-backtesting-theory counts the periods in which a
solver did not converge.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
res <- tryCatch(solve(matrix(0, 2, 2)), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
res
#> [1] "Lapackroutine dgesv: System ist genau singulär: U[1,1] = 0"
```
:::


## Plotting {.unnumbered}

The book plots with `ggplot2`, always from one data frame, and with the theme
set in `R/_common.R`. The grammar is a data frame, an aesthetic mapping, and
layers.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot2::ggplot(pts, ggplot2::aes(vol, ret, colour = kind)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 3) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = label), vjust = -1, size = 3) +
  scale_colour_tidyaa() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "volatility", y = "mean return")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}

:::

## Getting help {.unnumbered}

`?name` opens the help page of a function, `?package::name` when two packages
export the same name, and `args(name)` prints its signature. For the packages
this book is built on, `vignette(package = "PortfolioAnalytics")` lists the
worked examples that ship with the package, and @sec-93-package-notes says
which package the book reaches for in which situation.
